passage_text: Researchers conducted a randomized, double‑blind, placebo‑controlled trial to evaluate the effect of a novel antihypertensive agent, Hypertensol, on systolic blood pressure (SBP) in adults with stage 1 hypertension. Two hundred and forty patients were enrolled and randomly assigned to receive either Hypertensol (n=120) or a matching placebo (n=120) for 4 weeks. Baseline and 4‑week SBP and diastolic blood pressure (DBP) were measured in a standardized setting. The mean SBP at baseline was 148.2 mm Hg in the Hypertensol group and 147.9 mm Hg in the placebo group. After 4 weeks, the Hypertensol group’s mean SBP fell to 128.5 mm Hg, whereas the placebo group’s mean SBP was 146.3 mm Hg. Mean DBP decreased from 92.5 mm Hg to 84.7 mm Hg in the Hypertensol group and from 91.8 mm Hg to 90.9 mm Hg in the placebo group. The study concluded that Hypertensol lowers both SBP and DBP more than placebo, with a mean SBP reduction of 19.7 mm Hg in the treatment arm.
table_data:
Group | N | Mean SBP Baseline | Mean SBP 4w | Mean DBP Baseline | Mean DBP 4w
Hypertensol | 120 | 148.2 | 128.5 | 92.5 | 84.7
Placebo | 120 | 147.9 | 146.3 | 91.8 | 90.9
stem: What is the mean reduction in systolic blood pressure observed in the Hypertensol group?
explanation: Correct: A) The Hypertensol group fell from 148.2 to 128.5 mm Hg, a reduction of 19.7 mm Hg. Why the others are wrong: B) 18.1 mm Hg is the between-group difference (19.7 - 1.6), not the Hypertensol change. C) 15.6 mm Hg does not match the table. D) 12.3 mm Hg does not match the table.
trap: Subtracting the placebo fall of 1.6 mm Hg from the treatment fall gives 18.1 mm Hg, the net difference, but the question asks for the Hypertensol group's own reduction.

stem: Which experimental design best controls for potential confounding variables in this study?
explanation: Randomization and blinding minimize selection bias and placebo effect, making the double‑blind, placebo‑controlled trial the gold standard for controlling confounders.
trap: Choosing a cohort study with historical controls because it follows patients over time, although without randomization and concurrent placebo it cannot balance confounders.

stem: Calculate the percent reduction in mean systolic blood pressure in the Hypertensol group.
explanation: Correct: A) 19.7/148.2 x 100 = 13.3%, using the baseline as the denominator. Why the others are wrong: B) 15.3% divides by the 4-week value (128.5) instead of baseline. C) 12.1% does not follow from the table. D) 10.4% does not follow from the table.
trap: Dividing the 19.7 mm Hg fall by the follow-up SBP of 128.5 mm Hg (15.3%) instead of by the baseline of 148.2 mm Hg.

stem: Which of the following statements is FALSE regarding the study’s findings?

options.A: Hypertensol produced a greater reduction in SBP than placebo.
options.B: The placebo group’s SBP increased over the 4‑week period.
options.C: Both groups had similar baseline SBP values.
options.D: Hypertensol also lowered DBP compared with placebo.

explanation: The placebo group’s SBP decreased from 147.9 to 146.3 mm Hg, a modest reduction, not an increase.
trap: Rejecting D because the passage emphasises SBP; DBP fell 7.8 mm Hg with Hypertensol versus 0.9 with placebo, so D is true and the false statement is the claimed placebo rise in SBP.

stem: How much larger was the mean fall in SBP in the Hypertensol group than in the placebo group?
explanation: Correct: Hypertensol fell 148.2 to 128.5 (19.7) and placebo fell 147.9 to 146.3 (1.6); 19.7 minus 1.6 is 18.1 mm Hg. Why the others are wrong: A) this adds the two falls instead of subtracting. B) this is the Hypertensol fall alone. D) this is the placebo fall alone.
trap: Reporting the Hypertensol fall alone (19.7 mm Hg) without subtracting the placebo fall of 1.6 mm Hg, or adding the two falls to get 21.3 mm Hg.
